title: Sample quality control
overview_markdown:
**What you will do.** You will check the quality of every sample in the data. A sample is the DNA of one person. You will remove samples that are poor, mislabelled, repeated, related to another sample or measured on a faulty plate. At the end you will save a clean set of 1,844 samples.

**What you will learn.**

- How to find samples that failed in the laboratory.
- How to compare the recorded sex of a person with the sex shown by the DNA.
- How to find related people and repeated samples.
- How to find a plate that was measured badly.
- How to keep a record of every sample you remove, and why.

**How long it takes.** About 70 minutes. Step 3.6 is the slowest, because its rules for removing samples have the most detail.
recap_markdown:
- Rough cleaning removed three wells and 150 variants. The 98% call-rate rule then removed 42 more wells, leaving 1,971 samples.
- The sex check removed eight flagged wells, leaving 1,963 samples.
- The pruned subset has 69,539 sites. The heterozygosity check removed 13 low-F wells and flagged eight high-F wells, which we kept. 1,950 samples remained.
- The kinship check found 19 duplicate-class pairs and ten first-degree pairs. We removed 30 records, leaving 1,920 samples.
- Plate P14 had a lower call rate than the other plates. We removed its 76 remaining wells.
- The module ends with 1,844 samples and 296,360 variants, saved as the checkpoint at step 3.8.

**Next:** Module 4 checks the quality of the variants (variant QC).
